title: Passives and causatives
subtitle: The passive, impersonal passives, objects, avoiding the passive, have/get something done

rows.use: When we don't know who does/did something
rows.example: The prototype **was stolen** at approximately 1.30 am.

rows.use: When it's obvious who does/did something
rows.example: **Having been passed** in 1988, the Road Traffic Act regulates all vehicle use on UK roads.

rows.use: When it isn't important who does/did something
rows.example: The XL500 **was designed** with young families in mind, so there's plenty of room in the boot.

rows.use: To emphasise new information (which appears at the end of the sentence)
rows.example: This type of submarine **was developed** during the Second World War by the Americans.

rows.use: To avoid starting clauses with long expressions
rows.example: We **were surprised** by the number of people trying to leave the city for the long weekend. (More natural than The number of people trying to leave the city for the long weekend surprised us.)

rows.use: To produce a formal style
rows.example: All passengers **are required** to present their ticket to the inspector.

rows.use: noun + verb in passive form + infinitive / perfect infinitive
rows.example: Tourism **is expected to become** a major part of the country's economy. Common verbs: **agree, assume, believe, claim, consider, estimate, expect, feel, find, guarantee, know, mean, presume, regard, report, say, suppose, think, understand**

rows.use: There + verb in passive form + infinitive / perfect infinitive
rows.example: **There are reported to have been** a record number of accidents on the roads this year.

rows.use: It + verb in passive form + that clause
rows.example: **It is thought that** the new railway will provide employment opportunities for local people. Common verbs: **accept, agree, argue, assume, believe, calculate, claim, consider, estimate, expect, feel, know, presume, report, say, suggest, suppose, think, understand**

blocks.text: Some verbs in active sentences can be followed by both a direct and an indirect object (usually a person). Common verbs include: **bring, buy, get, give, leave, lend, make, offer, owe, pass, pay, promise, refuse, send, show, take, teach, tell, write**, etc. There are two possible passive forms.

rows.use: Active sentence
rows.example: Michael **gave** the plane tickets to Jill.

rows.use: With indirect object as subject of passive verb
rows.example: **Jill was given** the plane tickets (by Michael).

rows.use: With direct object as subject of passive verb
rows.example: **The plane tickets were given** to Jill (by Michael).

blocks.text: In the second structure, we sometimes omit the preposition before indirect object **pronouns**.
blocks.note: Sharon's Rolls-Royce **was left (to)** her by her grandfather.

blocks.text: With the verbs **explain** and **suggest**, the preposition before indirect object pronouns **cannot** be omitted. They cannot be used with the first structure in the table above.
blocks.note: How to drive the train **was explained to me**. (not **I was explained how to drive the train.** · not **How to drive the train was explained me.**)

blocks.text: The passive is not normally used with verbs in the present perfect continuous, past perfect continuous, future continuous or future perfect continuous tenses. Various prepositional phrases are used to avoid the passive in these tenses.

rows.use: in progress
rows.example: Preparations for the flight **will be in progress** as the President arrives at the airport. (not **will be being made**)

rows.use: in training
rows.example: By the end of this year, I **will have been in training** as a pilot for four years. (not **will have been being trained**)

rows.use: on display
rows.example: Vintage cars **have been on display** in the town centre all this week. (not **have been being displayed**)

rows.use: under consideration
rows.example: By the time they came to a decision, the problem **had been under consideration** for some time. (not **had been being considered**)

rows.use: under construction
rows.example: The new railway station **has been under construction** for two years now. (not **has been being built**)

blocks.text: Some verbs are not usually used in the passive. They include intransitive verbs such as **appear, arrive, die**, etc. Many verbs used statively are also not usually used in the passive. They include **consist, deserve, fit, have, lack, look, mind, realise, resemble, seem, suit**, etc.
The verb **let** is not used in the passive when it means 'allow', although phrasal verbs with **let** can be used in the passive.
blocks.note: Alice was clearly guilty, but she **was let off** with a warning.

blocks.text: Some verbs can be followed by the **bare infinitive** (without **to**) in active sentences. They are followed by the **full infinitive** in passive sentences. These verbs include **hear, help, make** and **see**.
blocks.note: We **heard** Jim **say** he was going to Albania. (active) · Jim **was heard to say** he was going to Albania. (passive)

rows.use: Actions we arrange for other people to do for us
rows.example: Did you finally **get** your bike **fixed**?

rows.use: Things we experience (usually negative and not intended)
rows.example: I heard that Susie **had** her motorbike **stolen**.

blocks.text: In general, **get** is more informal than **have** in causative structures. We can use other verbs instead of **get** and **have** with a causative meaning. They include **need, want** and **would like**.
blocks.note: I'd **like** those cars **washed** by this evening, please.

blocks.text: The structure **get something done** can also mean 'finish doing something'.
blocks.note: We'll set off as soon as I've **got** the car **fixed**.

rows.use: get somebody to do / have somebody do · actions we make somebody/something do for us
rows.example: Did you **get** Alex **to drive** you all the way to London?

rows.use: get/have somebody doing · actions we make somebody/something start doing
rows.example: Don't worry. We'll soon **have** your car **running** like new.

blocks.text: Most of the time, we do not show who does/did an action (the 'agent') in a passive or causative sentence. When we do want to refer to the agent, we use **by**.
blocks.note: We should **get** the car **looked at by** a professional.

blocks.text: When we want to refer to materials or instruments used in a passive or causative sentence, we use **with**.
blocks.note: The engine **is started with** a special electronic card instead of a key.

blocks.text: We use other prepositions after some past participles that are used like adjectives.
blocks.note: I am **frightened of** driving on motorways. · My car is **covered in** dirt.

exercises.title: D · Heathrow
exercises.instruction: Each sentence contains one verb in the wrong form. Rewrite the incorrect word or phrase correctly.

items.prompt: Heathrow Airport, near London, has called the world's busiest international airport and the 68 million passengers who **are processed** each year would probably agree.
The land on which the airport stands **sold** to Fairey Aviation by the local vicar and was used for test flights during the 1930s, under the name Great Western Aerodrome.
In 1944, the airport **was handed** over to the government and was developed for civilian use, was named after a small village that was removed to create space, Heath Row.
The first concrete slab of the modern runways **laid** by Queen Elizabeth II in 1953, and the first terminal building, which has later renamed Terminal 2, was opened two years later.
The London Underground **was extended** to reach Heathrow in 1977, meaning that passengers could be transport from central London via the Piccadilly Line in just under an hour.
Four passenger terminals and a cargo terminal **have been constructed** and permission was been granted for a fifth passenger terminal in 2001.

It has been suggested that a new airport, which would lead to Heathrow **being retired** over a period of 20 years, has been built on a floating island in the Thames, although no firm plans have been drawn up.

exercises.title: E · Avoiding the passive
exercises.instruction: Complete the sentences describing each situation using the phrase given.

items.prompt:
I started training to be an accountant six months ago. I've got six more months to go, and then I have to take some exams. **in training**
By the time I take my exams, ___ .
acceptedAnswers: I will have been in training for a year
I'll have been in training for a year
I will have been in training as an accountant for a year

items.prompt:
The council have been thinking for some time of redeveloping the city centre. **under consideration**
The redevelopment of the city centre ___ .
acceptedAnswers: has been under consideration for some time

items.prompt:
They've been having discussions on the issue for over two weeks. **in progress**
Discussions on the issue ___ .
acceptedAnswers: have been in progress for over two weeks
have been in progress for more than two weeks

items.prompt:
This weekend, the local Art Society will be displaying their latest works at the library. **on display**
The local Art Society's latest works ___ .
acceptedAnswers: will be on display at the library this weekend
will be on display this weekend

items.prompt:
George seems to have been putting his website together for a long time. **under construction**
George's website ___ .
acceptedAnswers: has been under construction for a long time
seems to have been under construction for a long time

exercises.title: F · Causative dialogue
exercises.instruction: If the word or phrase in bold is correct, write a tick (✓). If it is incorrect, rewrite it correctly.

items.prompt: Alison: Oh, what a nightmare! We had to **have it repaired** twice!
Alison: Well, we got **delivered it** to our house on Monday morning.
Hannah: We decided to have it **check** straight away, because it had come all the way from America.
Alison: Oh, I didn't know you'd had them **do that**.
Alison: Yeah. Anyway, we had my dad **to have a look** at it. And he found that the engine wasn't running properly.
Hannah: Did you have the company **to come** to fix it?
Alison: Well, not at first. I bet we got my brother **to work** on it.
Alison: Oh, he's very good. I bet he soon had **running it** smoothly.
Alison: Yes, but we still had to get the company **come** out in the end, because the fuel pump stopped working.
Hannah: Terrible! You should get them **to give** you some compensation.
